nameStory: The storey anemone gets its name from its unusual ability to build itself up in layers or 'storeys' like floors of a building. This sea anemone can actually reproduce by budding off new individuals that remain attached, creating a multi-level colony that resembles a tiny underwater apartment complex.
description: The storey anemone is a fascinating sea creature that looks like an underwater flower but is actually an animal. It has a soft, cylindrical body topped with a crown of tentacles that wave gently in the current. Unlike most sea anemones that live as single individuals, this species often forms connected colonies where multiple anemones stack and cluster together. It's found on both sides of the northern Atlantic Ocean, making it one of the few sea anemones with such a wide distribution.

idTips.label: Colony formation
idTips.description: Look for multiple anemones clustered or stacked together in connected groups, rather than single isolated individuals

idTips.label: Tentacle arrangement
idTips.description: Tentacles form a neat crown around the mouth, feeling soft and slightly sticky to gentle touch when extended underwater

idTips.label: Body texture
idTips.description: The column (body) feels smooth and somewhat squishy, like a firm grape, and can contract when disturbed

idTips.label: Attachment style
idTips.description: Firmly attached to hard surfaces like rocks or shells, with individuals often sharing a common base in colonies

idTips.label: Response to touch
idTips.description: Quickly retracts tentacles and contracts into a tight, rounded blob when gently poked or disturbed

habitat: Look for storey anemones in New England's rocky intertidal zones and shallow subtidal waters, particularly along the Maine coast. They prefer hard surfaces like rock faces, large boulders, or shells where they can establish their colonies. You'll often find them in areas with good water circulation, from the low tide line down to moderate depths.

seasonality.spring: Colonies become more active as water temperatures rise, with tentacles more frequently extended for feeding. Good time to observe their colonial structure as they expand after winter dormancy.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when tentacles are most often extended and visible. Reproduction and budding of new individuals in colonies is most likely during warmer months.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to contract more frequently as temperatures drop. Colonies may appear more compact as individual anemones prepare for winter.
seasonality.winter: Often contracted and less active, appearing as small bumps or mounds. Colonies may be harder to distinguish from surrounding growth, but the clustered pattern is still visible.

funFact: The storey anemone is like nature's apartment building - when it reproduces, the babies don't move out! Instead, they stay attached to their parent, creating multi-generational family towers that can contain dozens of individuals all sharing the same foundation, making it one of the few sea anemones that truly lives in a commune.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small sea anemones, but the key difference is the clustering habit - if you see multiple anemones growing together in a connected group rather than scattered individually, you're likely looking at storey anemones. Remember: storey anemones stick together, while most other species live alone.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called the 'storey anemone,' it's not related to the architectural term 'story' meaning floor levels, but rather refers to its stacked, multi-level growth pattern. This species represents the only member of its entire genus, making it quite unique in the sea anemone world.
compareHints: Since this is the only species in its genus Gonactinia, it's most similar to other colonial sea anemones in different families. However, most sea anemones in New England waters live as solitary individuals, making the storey anemone's colonial clustering behavior its most distinctive feature. Unlike other anemones that might accidentally group together due to favorable conditions, storey anemones are truly connected and share resources through their joined bases.
